Your Groceries Cost 32% More. Why?

2026-11-24

Subscribe for one money story a week

About this video

U.S. grocery prices (CPI food at home) are up 32.5% since January 2020, and this year's classic Thanksgiving dinner for 10 costs $58.63, more than 6% above last year, with the 16-lb turkey up 10%, per the American Farm Bureau. Coffee is up 122% ($4.17 to $9.25 a pound), ground beef 74%, eggs 59% after peaking at $6.23 a dozen. We look at why food costs more (fuel, labor, packaging: under 6 cents of each grocery dollar reaches the farm), groceries vs your other bills, and whether pay kept up (average hourly pay +33.7%). 0:00 Your groceries: +32% 0:33 Thanksgiving, line by line 1:19 What happened after 2021? 1:48 Is eating out the answer? 2:07 The item that doubled 2:45 How high did it go? 3:07 Why burgers cost more 3:31 Only 6 cents to the farm? 4:08 The price that crashed 4:32 Did your pay keep up? 5:13 Bills that beat your pay 5:50 What it costs you a year 6:11 How many hours per cart? 6:42 What got cheaper 6:57 The credit card trap 7:20 4 ways to cut the bill 7:43 Recap Sources: BLS consumer price indexes and average prices via FRED (CUSR0000SAF11, CPIAUCSL, CUSR0000SEFV, CUSR0000SEHA, CUSR0000SEHF01, CUSR0000SETA02, APU0000717311, APU0000703112, APU0000708111, APU0000702111, APU0000709112, APU0000711211), BLS average hourly earnings (CES0500000003), EIA weekly gas price (GASREGW), Federal Reserve G.19 credit card rate (TERMCBCCINTNS); American Farm Bureau Federation 2026 Thanksgiving dinner survey (Nov 18, 2026). Diesel for the trucks and tractors. A shortage of farm workers. And the cost of processing, packaging and shipping everything. Here's the part most people don't know: by the USDA's estimate, less than 6 cents of every dollar you spend on groceries goes back to the farmer. The rest pays for everything that happens after the farm. Turkey has its own story. Still higher than 2020, but way off the peak. When supply recovers, prices can fall fast. Now the big question. Did your pay keep up? Since January 2020, grocery prices rose 32.5 percent. So if you put 500 dollars of holiday shopping on a card and leave it there for a year, you'd pay about 124 dollars in interest. That can wipe out the discount you were chasing. So what can you actually do? These are the habits consumer experts recommend most. Compare the unit price on the shelf tag, not the sticker price: it shows the cost per ounce or per pound. Try store brands, which usually cost less for similar products. Plan the week's meals so less food gets thrown away. And frozen fruit and vegetables keep longer and often cost less than fresh.
